# Abstract

Reconstructing long-run human population across Mesoamerica, the Central American isthmus, the Antilles and Bermuda requires bridging three structurally dissimilar evidentiary worlds: prehistoric archaeological settlement surveys and radiocarbon sequences, sixteenth- to nineteenth-century colonial fiscal, parish and plantation enumerations, and republican to contemporary national censuses. Global gridded datasets such as HYDE allocate historical national totals onto 5-arcminute grids using biophysical suitability rules and static fractional weights [@KleinGoldewijk2017], whereas continental demographic syntheses report aggregate trajectories inside modern sovereign boundaries [@McEvedyJones1978; @Maddison2001; @LiviBacci2007]. Across a 2,92M km² domain stretching from the arid basins of northern Mexico and the volcanic highlands of Mesoamerica to the lowland karst of the Maya Petén, the Chibchan isthmus and the Antillean island arc, backward projection of contemporary national borders and modern urban weights distorts both the pre-Columbian demographic geography and the spatially asymmetric collapse after 1492. JAGUAR resolves these distortions from 10000BC to 2025 through a bottom-up spatial-demographic reconstruction uniting archaeological site density, dual land-use priors, period-authentic historical administrative boundaries and evidence-only settlement gazetteers.

JAGUAR integrates 28 constituent chapter documents (14 regional and chronological literature reviews paired with 14 coordinate-anchored settlement gazetteers), supported by 238 SHA-256-unique open-access scholarly PDFs, 15.401 settlement trajectories (14.702 city-proper records and 699 preserved extra-municipal suburbs under municipal non-decomposition for unified Ciudad de México) and 3.785 primary historical sub-administrative enumerations spanning 543 administrative units and 29 territorial regimes across all 118 overlapping Common Era HYDE epochs from 0AD to 2025. Pre-statistical surfaces combine 11.970 domestic archaeological sites (19,98 times the baseline radiocarbon inventory, 99,19% primary regional institutional provenance and 0,0% crowd-sourced fallback) plus 1.248 CENTAUR northern frontier buffer sites across 1.673 dual HYDE 3.5 and KK10 catchments within a non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) residual kriging model ($\tau_1 = 1,35$, zero uninhabitable landmass leakage). From 1500 to 2025, pycnophylactic mass-conserving dasymetric scaling across non-anachronistic historical GIS boundaries achieves a maximum sub-administrative unit relative error of $5,76 \times 10^{-8}$ across 103 scaled rasters.

Across the 2,92M km² JAGUAR domain, gridded population rose from 480,1k in 10000BC and 1,39M in 6000BC to 2,93M by 1000BC as sedentary maize farming consolidated across the Mexican highlands, Oaxaca, the Gulf coast and the Maya lowlands. Classic and Post-Classic urbanisation carried domain totals from 2,03M in 1AD and 2,95M in 1000AD to 4,99M in 1500AD, before Eurasian pathogens, famine and colonial disruption halved the gridded population to 2,50M by 1600AD (with steeper local collapses exceeding 80% in the Greater Antilles and tropical coastal lowlands). Colonial demographic recovery and transatlantic plantation settlement restored domain numbers to 4,69M in 1700, 6,18M in 1800 and 7,23M in 1850; republican census harmonisation and twentieth-century mortality decline then lifted JAGUAR totals to 17,67M in 1900, 40,56M in 1950, 137,20M in 1990, 189,89M in 2010 and 201,93M in 2025.

# Background

Long-run population reconstruction across Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and Bermuda poses four distinct cartographic and statistical problems that global gridded inventories cannot resolve cleanly from national-level series alone [@KleinGoldewijk2017; @McEvedyJones1978; @Maddison2001]. Unlike temperate Eurasian river plains where demographic centres remained spatially persistent across millennia, the JAGUAR macro-region underwent three radical geographical inversions between the mid-Holocene and the twenty-first century.

First, pre-Columbian demographic density did not align with contemporary sovereign frontiers or modern industrial coastlines. Dense Formative, Classic and Post-Classic societies concentrated in highland volcanic basins (the Basin of Mexico, the Puebla-Tlaxcala valley, Oaxaca and the Guatemalan highlands), fertile Gulf alluvial corridors, the karst lowlands of the Petén and northern Yucatán, and the coastal and interior valleys of Hispaniola and Puerto Rico [@SandersParsonsSantley1979; @Blanton1999; @CulbertRice1990; @KeeganHofman2017]. Modern borders such as the straight-line boundaries separating Mexico, Guatemala and Belize across the Petén forest, or the northern meridian separating Baja California from Sonora, cut directly through unified pre-Columbian hydrological and cultural zones. When gridded reconstructions disaggregate modern country totals backward into 1000BC or 800AD, artificial density cliffs emerge along geometric lines that did not exist before nineteenth- and twentieth-century treaties.

Second, the sixteenth-century demographic collapse following European contact was neither uniform across space nor synchronous across ecological zones [@BorahCook1963; @CookBorah1971; @Denevan1992; @Whitmore1992; @Koch2019]. In the Greater Antilles, epidemic mortality, forced labour and social dislocation eliminated the vast majority of the indigenous Taíno population within two generations of 1492 [@Sauer1966; @Henige1978; @LiviBacci2003; @AndersonCordova2017]. On the Mesoamerican mainland, repeated epidemics of smallpox, measles and haemorrhagic *huey cocoliztli* (including documented *Salmonella enterica* outbreaks during megadrought intervals) struck tropical coasts and highland basins with sharply differing intensities between 1519 and 1650 [@Gibson1964; @Brooks1993; @AcunaSoto2002; @Vagene2018; @Lovell1992; @Newson1986]. Representing this transformation through a single national multiplier erases the divergence between depopulated lowlands (such as the Petén, Veracruz and Hispaniola), resilient indigenous highland cores (such as Oaxaca, Chiapas and the Cuchumatán mountains) and newly founded colonial silver-mining cities across the Bajío and northern Zacatecas [@Brading1971; @Gerhard1993; @MinoGrijalva2001].

Third, between 1650 and 1898 the Caribbean basin experienced a second demographic inversion driven by the transatlantic slave trade and imperial sugar economies [@EltisRichardson2010; @EngermanHigman1997; @Higman1984]. Small islands that had held modest pre-contact numbers or had been nearly emptied after 1520 (Barbados, Jamaica, Martinique, Guadeloupe, Saint-Domingue and western Cuba) rapidly attained some of the highest rural densities in the Western Hemisphere, while Bermuda developed a distinct maritime parish demography in the western Atlantic [@Kuczynski1953; @Roberts1957; @Geggus1997; @MoreauStMery1797]. Accurate spatial gridding across this period requires island-specific colonial enumerations and period-authentic imperial frontiers, including the 1697-1795 Hispaniola partition and the 1822-1844 Haitian unification of the island, rather than late twentieth-century Caribbean state aggregates.

Fourth, modern census integration across 37 sovereign and dependent jurisdictions suffers from inconsistent urban definitions and administrative fragmentation. In Mexico, treating the 16 constituent *alcaldías* of Ciudad de México as separate cities artificially dismantles the hemisphere's largest highland metropolis, whereas conflating municipal-level totals with city-proper cores distorts rank-size scaling across Central America and the Antilles [@Unikel1976; @Garza2003; @INEGICPV2021; @CONAPO2023]. JAGUAR addresses all four challenges simultaneously, maintaining continuous northern frontier harmonisation along the 250 km US-Mexico seam with CENTAUR while preserving strictly regional archaeological, colonial and republican statistical foundations.

# Methodology

## Canonical 14-Chapter Architecture and Areal Masking

JAGUAR partitions its 2,92M km² terrestrial domain (exact area 2.923.591 km², covering 35.104 valid 5-arcminute cells) into 14 chronological and regional chapters arranged into three major historical groups (Table 1 and Figure 1). Every chapter pairs a regional demographic literature review with a coordinate-anchored settlement gazetteer, a 4320x2160 pixel equal-area mask, a vector sub-regional partition, a provenance ledger and an archived scholarly library of 16 to 18 unique open-access PDFs across at least nine distinct institutional domains.

The first five chapters cover Pre-Columbian societies from 10000BC to European contact. Chapter 1 spans Pre-Columbian Mesoamerica to 1200AD across 1,79M km² and seven non-Maya ecological zones derived strictly from organic HydroBASINS watershed divides, tracing Palaeoindian foraging through Olmec, Teotihuacan, Zapotec and Toltec urbanism [@Diehl2004; @Pool2007; @Millon1973; @Cowgill2015; @Mastache2002]. Chapter 2 isolates the Classic and Post-Classic Maya lands (2000BC-1524AD, 471,0k km², six ecological zones) across northern Yucatán, the Petén-Usumacinta basin, Belize, highland Chiapas, highland Guatemala and the Motagua-Copán corridor with zero modern international straight lines [@CulbertRice1990; @SharerTraxler2006; @HoustonInomata2009; @Canuto2018]. Chapter 3 models the Aztec Empire and Late Post-Classic Mexico (1200AD-1519AD, 1,79M km², eight indigenous polity zones separating the Basin of Mexico, Tlaxcala, Purépecha Michoacán, Mixtec-Zapotec Oaxaca, the Huasteca, West Mexico and Aridoamerica) [@Carrasco1999; @Pollard1993; @Smith2008AztecCity; @Berdan2014]. Chapters 4 and 5 extend coverage across Pre-Columbian Lower Central America (10000BC-1502AD, 386,9k km², six Chibchan and isthmian watershed zones from eastern Honduras to Gran Darién) and the Pre-Columbian Caribbean Islands (5000BC-1492AD, 321,0k km², seven archipelagic zones from western Cuba and Hispaniola to the Lucayan Bahamas, Lesser Antilles and Trinidad) [@Cooke2005; @Hoopes2005; @Rouse1992; @Wilson2007; @Siegel2015].

Chapters 6 through 10 document Conquest, demographic collapse and colonial restructuring between 1492 and 1898. Chapter 6 captures Conquest and Collapse in Mexico and Central America (1518-1650, 2,60M km², seven early colonial *audiencia* and frontier zones), while Chapter 9 tracks the Spanish Conquest of the Indigenous Caribbean across the Antilles (1492-1650, 321,0k km², six zones anchored on the *Audiencia de Santo Domingo*) [@CookBorah1971; @Whitmore1992; @DeaganCruxent2002; @LiviBacci2003]. Chapters 7 and 8 then trace the mature colonial administrations of the Viceroyalty of New Spain (1535-1821, 1,97M km², 12 Bourbon intendancies and *Provincias Internas*) and the Captaincy General of Guatemala and Central America including Chiapas, Panama and early British Honduras (1524-1821, 682,9k km², eight zones with an organic Honduras-Mosquitia watershed divide) [@Gerhard1962; @Gerhard1993; @MacLeod1973; @Wortman1982; @HallPerezBrignoli2003]. Chapter 10 spans the Colonial Caribbean Plantation Era (1650-1898, 321,6k km², nine imperial zones including the historical 1697-1795 Hispaniola frontier and Bermuda at 32,3°N, 64,8°W) [@Higman1984; @EngermanHigman1997; @Geggus1997].

Finally, Chapters 11 through 14 cover Republican, Post-Emancipation and Modern Census demography through 2025: Mexico after Independence (Chapter 11, 1821-2025, 2,06M km², nine federal macro-zones covering all 32 states), the Central American Republics after Independence including the 1903-1979 Panama Canal Zone footprint (Chapter 12, 1821-2025, 587,3k km², eight zones), the Greater Antilles in the Modern Era across Cuba, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Jamaica and Puerto Rico (Chapter 13, 1838-2025, 253,7k km², seven zones) and the Lesser Antilles, Bahamas, Trinidad and Bermuda (Chapter 14, 1838-2025, 67,8k km², ten island groupings) [@INEGICensos1996; @Alba1982; @PerezBrignoli2010; @DiazBriquets1983; @VazquezCalzada1988; @BSOBermuda2018].

```{r tab-chapters, results='asis'}
ch_list <- root_summary$chapters
df_ch <- data.frame(
  Ch = sapply(ch_list, function(x) sprintf("%02d", as.integer(x$index))),
  Module = sapply(ch_list, function(x) x$title),
  Span = sapply(ch_list, function(x) {
    d0 <- as.integer(x$domain[[1]])
    d1 <- as.integer(x$domain[[2]])
    s0 <- if (d0 < 0) paste0(abs(d0), "BC") else as.character(d0)
    s1 <- if (d1 < 0) paste0(abs(d1), "BC") else as.character(d1)
    paste0(s0, "-", s1)
  }),
  Area_km2 = sapply(ch_list, function(x) viscount_fmt_pop(x$area_km2)),
  Zones = sapply(ch_list, function(x) as.character(x$subregions)),
  Setts = sapply(ch_list, function(x) formatC(as.integer(x$settlement_count), format = "d", big.mark = ".")),
  Zipf = sapply(ch_list, function(x) viscount_fmt_number(x$zipf_alpha, 2L)),
  PDFs = sapply(ch_list, function(x) as.character(x$archival_pdfs)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_ch) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_ch,
  "Canonical 14-chapter itinerary of JAGUAR showing chronological spans, equal-area footprints, regional zones, settlement counts, rank-size exponents and archived scholarly PDFs.",
  c("Ch.", "Regional or Chronological Module", "Span", "Area (km²)", "Zones", "Setts", "Zipf", "PDFs"),
  list(label = "tab:jaguar-chapters", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Archaeological Substrata and Non-Stationary Matérn Kriging

Pre-statistical spatial surfaces from 10000BC through 1850AD, together with rural sub-district weights in later epochs, rely on a continental archaeological corpus compiled specifically for JAGUAR without any crowd-sourced demographic reliance. Across all 35 countries and territories in the domain, ingestion and cross-repository deduplication yielded 11.970 unique domestic archaeological sites, representing 19,98 times the baseline global radiocarbon inventory of 599 deduplicated sites. Of these domestic records, 11.873 sites (99,19%) derive from 15 distinct primary regional monographs and national heritage registers (11.743 monograph sites, 130 national heritage register sites and 97 radiocarbon database anchors), with 0,0% crowd-sourced fallback. By macro-jurisdiction, Mexico contributes 8.619 sites (99,95% primary regional across ten sources), Central America contributes 2.969 sites (99,56% primary regional across nine sources) and the Caribbean and Bermuda contribute 382 sites (79,06% primary regional across seven sources). To prevent boundary edge effects along the northern desert seam, 1.248 CENTAUR frontier sites within a 250 km northern buffer across the US Southwest, Texas and southern California join the kriging matrix (13.218 total sites, Table 2).

The principal archaeological archives include the Witschey and Brown FAMSI MayaGIS Electronic Atlas (3.246 sites), the UCSB Maya Forest GIS (2.424 sites), the sixteenth-century *Relaciones Geográficas* and *Suma de Visitas* historical gazetteer from Digging into Early Colonial Mexico (2.416 sites), the Harvard Dataverse Archaeological Atlas of Published Excavations (1.572 sites), the Basin of Mexico Settlement Pattern Survey (1.292 sites), the University of Pittsburgh Comparative Archaeology Database regional surveys across Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama, Chiapas and Veracruz (348 sites), the Southwest Social Networks database for Chihuahua and Sonora (294 sites), the Allen Ancient DNA Resource (73 directly dated sites including pre-contact Caribbean genomic samples), the Mexican INAH official register (70 sites), the DANS NEXUS1492 Montecristi Coast survey in the northern Dominican Republic (69 sites), UNESCO World Heritage properties (31 sites), audited archaeological sites from the US National Park Service NRHP register in Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands (24 sites) and early colonial surveyed parishes of Bermuda (eight sites) [@SandersParsonsSantley1979; @Fernandes2021; @Nagele2020; @Fitzpatrick2015]. Rigorous pre-kriging cleaning merged 11.126 cross-repository duplicates, stripped 257 natural physiographic features from the colonial gazetteer and 382 non-archaeological modern buildings from Caribbean registers, replaced 164 placeholder register dates and collapsed 864 stacked island-centroid radiocarbon records while matching 41 fuzzed Caribbean radiocarbon dates to true field coordinates.

Site intensities were aggregated onto 1.673 domestic geodesic Voronoi catchments (1.449 active domestic catchments, 86,61% catchment coverage ratio, median radius 21,65 km, 90th-percentile radius 31,95 km) plus 144 CENTAUR frontier catchments, paired with dual HYDE 3.5 and KK10 biophysical suitability covariates [@KleinGoldewijk2017]. Across nine chronological strata (Palaeoindian-Archaic, Early-Middle Pre-Classic Olmec, Late Pre-Classic Teotihuacan rise, Classic Mesoamerica and Maya peak, Epi-Classic and Early Post-Classic Toltec, Late Post-Classic Aztec and Taíno, Conquest epidemic collapse, Bourbon colonial plantation and Independence pre-census), JAGUAR fits weighted least-squares environmental trend models (habitability, natural vegetation, ecological productivity, fluvial proximity and coastal access) and interpolates log-intensity residuals via non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging [@PaciorekSchervish2006]. Calibration sets the dimensionless short-range correlation parameter to $\tau_1 = 1,35$ (long-range $\tau_2 = 2,9025$, effective short-range scale 34,35 km to 37,18 km, nugget-to-sill ratio 0,04, component weights $c_1 = 0,80$ and $c_2 = 0,20$) alongside a two-cell urban mask buffer to prevent twentieth-century metropolitan sprawl from back-projecting into pre-industrial strata (Figure 2).

The fitted weighted least-squares covariate coefficients trace clear ecological transitions across the Holocene without requiring manual regional tuning. During the Palaeoindian-Archaic horizon (10000BC-3000BC), coastal access ($\beta_4 = 0,0853$) and fluvial proximity ($\beta_3 = 0,0806$) exert their strongest spatial pull alongside baseline habitability ($\beta_0 = 0,0354$), reflecting foraging mobility along estuaries, highland lake margins and alluvial corridors. As highland rain-fed and terraced agriculture intensified from the Pre-Classic through the Late Post-Classic, fluvial weights fell monotonically from $0,0596$ (Late Pre-Classic) and $0,0422$ (Classic Maya peak) to $0,0143$ (Epi-Classic Toltec) and $0,0100$ (Late Post-Classic Aztec and Taíno), while coastal weights softened from $0,0762$ to $0,0336$, registering the shift of demographic mass into interior volcanic valleys and karst uplands. Immediately following 1519, sixteenth-century demographic collapse and early Spanish port-and-road reorganisation drove a transient rebound in fluvial ($\beta_3 = 0,0834$) and coastal ($\beta_4 = 0,0630$) coefficients during the Conquest stratum before colonial inland mining and agricultural integration moderated both terms again through 1821.

## Non-Anachronistic Historical GIS Sub-Administrative Architecture

Across all 118 overlapping Common Era HYDE epochs from 0AD to 2025, JAGUAR replaces uniform national downscaling with a strictly non-anachronistic historical GIS architecture spanning 29 distinct boundary regimes, 60 primary statistical and archival sources, 543 enumerated administrative units and 3.785 primary sub-administrative observations (5.768 total compiled rows) across 37 jurisdictions (Table 3, Table 4 and Figure 3). Every polygon geometry matches the authentic territorial boundaries of its epoch, prohibiting backward projection of twentieth-century provincial or state splits into colonial or nineteenth-century rasters.

Prior to 1500, sub-regional partitions follow pure organic HydroBASINS watersheds across Mexico and Central America alongside intact island territories across the Caribbean and Bermuda (27 active units in 1500). In 1600, colonial *audiencias* and early Spanish governorships (33 active units) preserve a unified Baja California peninsula without the modern 28°N boundary and exclude any anachronistic Belize enclave. By 1700-1800, coverage expands to 57-59 units capturing the 12 Bourbon intendancies and *Provincias Internas* of New Spain (anchored on Gerhard's 1742 reconstruction, the 1790 Revillagigedo census and Humboldt's 1803 tables), the provinces of the Captaincy General of Guatemala (Juarros 1808 and Bishop Cortés y Larraz returns), divided colonial Hispaniola along its 1697-1795 frontier, four Cuban jurisdictions and British, French, Dutch and Danish plantation islands [@Gerhard1962; @SPPRevillagigedo1977; @Humboldt1811; @Juarros1808; @Kuczynski1953; @DanishWestIndies1912].

Following independence, territorial snapshots follow constitutional realignments closely: the 1824 Mexican Constitution states (unified Occidente combining Sonora and Sinaloa, unified Yucatán and undivided Estado de México) alongside Haiti's 1822-1844 unification of Hispaniola; mid-nineteenth-century creation of Guerrero and Campeche (147 active units in 1850); late nineteenth-century republican censuses including Busto (1880), García Cubas (1884), Costa Rica (1864-1892), Honduras (1881-1895), Guatemala (1893) and the 1899 US War Department censuses of Cuba and Puerto Rico (297-302 active units in 1890-1900) [@Busto1880; @GarciaCubas1884; @Davidson2002; @USWarDeptCuba1900; @USWarDeptPR1900]. Twentieth-century snapshots faithfully introduce Quintana Roo only after 1902, the Panama Canal Zone strictly from 1903 to 1979 (reverting to Panama in 1980), the 28°N Baja California partition only after 1931, and modern splits including Cuba's Artemisa and Mayabeque provinces after 2011 and Panamá Oeste after 2014 [@INEGIEHM2015; @USCensusCanalZone1973; @ONEICuba2014; @INECPanama2023]. Within every polygon across all 103 post-1500 scaled rasters, pycnophylactic dasymetric scaling iteratively adjusts 5-arcminute suitability cells so cell sums reproduce every recorded sub-administrative total exactly.

```{r tab-hgis-regimes, results='asis'}
eras <- root_summary$subadmin_hgis_coverage$era_breakdown
era_labels <- c(
  "Colonial New Spain (1570-1810)",
  "Colonial Central America (1778-1816)",
  "Colonial Caribbean and Bermuda (1655-1899)",
  "Mexican Republic (1820-1889)",
  "Mexico INEGI Censuses (1895-2020)",
  "Central American Republics (1864-2024)",
  "Greater Antilles Historic (1899-1979)",
  "Greater Antilles Modern (1935-2023)",
  "Lesser Antilles, Bahamas and Bermuda (1900-2025)"
)
df_hgis <- data.frame(
  Series = era_labels,
  Span = sapply(eras, function(x) paste0(x$year_min, "-", x$year_max)),
  Jurisd = sapply(eras, function(x) as.character(x$jurisdictions)),
  Units = sapply(eras, function(x) formatC(as.integer(x$units), format = "d", big.mark = ".")),
  Obs = sapply(eras, function(x) formatC(as.integer(x$observations), format = "d", big.mark = ".")),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_hgis) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_hgis,
  "Compiled primary historical GIS sub-administrative census series across the 29 non-anachronistic territorial regimes of JAGUAR (543 units and 3.785 observations across 37 jurisdictions).",
  c("Historical Census Series", "Year Span", "Territories", "Units", "Observations"),
  list(label = "tab:hgis-eras", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

```{r tab-hgis-snapshots, results='asis'}
    "Early colonial audiencias; unified Baja California; zero Belize wedge",

  ),

)

  list(label = "tab:hgis-snapshots", font_size = "footnotesize")
```

## Evidence-Only Settlement Gazetteers and Metropolitan Reconciliation

Across all 14 chapters, JAGUAR compiles 15.401 strictly evidence-based settlement trajectories (14.702 city-proper records and 699 preserved extra-municipal suburbs) with zero synthetic interpolation and 0,0% crowd-sourced demographic authority. Primary harvest ingested 125 raw archival and statistical files (141,6 MB) containing 792.805 official and academic demographic rows: 762.027 raw INEGI ITER locality records spanning 1990-2020 across 297.902 unique Mexican localities (consolidated to 12.383 localities of at least 1.000 inhabitants or municipal seats), 683 historical city-year records from INEGI *Estadísticas Históricas de México* (31 cities, 1742-2010), 1.651 colonial settlements from HGIS de las Indias, 2.512 UNSD Demographic Yearbook city-year records, 4.827 HDX/OCHA sub-national census rows across Central America and the Caribbean, 1.640 US Census Puerto Rico records, 494 US Virgin Islands records, 68 INSEE French Antilles commune returns and national census publications from every Caribbean and isthmian statistical office [@INEGICPV2021; @INEGIEHM2015; @UNSDHistorical2000; @USCensusPR2024; @USCensusUSVI2021; @INSEEDOM2024].

To avoid municipal distortion in major conurbations, JAGUAR enforces strict municipal non-decomposition paired with a three-phase metropolitan reconciliation protocol. Under municipal non-decomposition, unified Ciudad de México consolidates all 16 constituent *alcaldías* of the former Distrito Federal as a single city-proper entity (8,24M in 1990, 8,61M in 2000, 8,85M in 2010 and 9,21M in 2020), preventing artificial fragmentation of the national capital while preserving 657 extra-municipal suburbs across the surrounding Valley of Mexico, Guadalajara, Monterrey and Puebla metropolitan belts (plus 17 suburbs in Central America, 17 in the Greater Antilles and eight in the Lesser Antilles, Bahamas and Bermuda) as subordinate records linked explicitly to their host cores. Phase 1 normalises city-proper census boundaries; Phase 2 deduplicates variant spellings and merges overlapping municipal tracts within metropolitan cores; Phase 3 reconciles city-proper trajectories against aggregate sub-administrative and national totals so urban shares never exceed their enclosing district populations.

# Testing and Validation

Validation of JAGUAR rests on five quantitative benchmarks covering archaeological provenance, Matérn kriging fidelity, sub-administrative mass conservation, northern frontier continuity and settlement gazetteer integrity (Table 5).

First, archaeological substrata audits confirmed 11.970 unique domestic sites (19,98 times the 599-site radiocarbon baseline, far above the 2,5 times threshold), 99,19% primary regional institutional provenance overall (99,95% in Mexico, 99,56% in Central America and 79,06% in the Caribbean and Bermuda), 0,0% crowd-sourced records across every jurisdiction, zero null or malformed dates and zero out-of-mask domestic points. Across all 1.673 domestic Voronoi catchments, 1.449 catchments (86,61%) carry active archaeological site observations, complemented by 144 northern buffer catchments populated by 1.248 CENTAUR sites.

Second, non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging calibration across all nine chronological strata achieved residual variogram fits of $R^2 = 0,9990$ to $0,9996$ (effective short-range scales 34,35 km to 37,18 km, dimensionless $\tau_1 = 1,35$, nugget-to-sill ratio $0,04$) with 0,0000 uninhabitable landmass leakage. Visual and texture inspection of the 5-arcminute outputs confirmed crisp topographic alignment along the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, Oaxaca valleys, Yucatán-Petén lowlands and Antillean coastlines, with zero isotropic Voronoi blobs, zero Manhattan diamond artefacts, high-pass spatial contrast averaging 0,3232 on kriged surfaces (0,3154 on final scaled rasters) and maximum directional anisotropy of 1,2239.

Third, automated pycnophylactic verification across all 103 post-1500 scaled rasters (1500 to 2025) confirmed strict mass conservation: total actual raster sums matched target administrative sums to eight significant figures in every year, with a worst sub-administrative unit relative error of $5,76 \times 10^{-8}$ and a worst country-level relative error of $5,22 \times 10^{-8}$ (nearly five orders of magnitude tighter than the $10^{-3}$ tolerance). Separate mask auditing verified all 14 chapter masks and 11 historical sub-administrative regime snapshots (1500 through 2020) for zero anachronistic state borders, zero coastal gaps and intact 10x Bermuda insets.

Fourth, northern frontier harmonisation blended 322 border pixels along the Rio Grande, Sonoran and Baja California seam with CENTAUR across 52 time steps, eliminating cross-border density discontinuities between northern Mexico and the southwestern United States.

Fifth, settlement gazetteer checks passed across all 14 chapters (15.401 trajectories, zero empty regional zones, zero crowd-sourced population figures, unified Ciudad de México non-decomposition and 238 SHA-256-unique archived scholarly PDFs with a minimum of 16 PDFs and nine institutional domains per chapter).

# Results

## Long-Run Holocene Demographic Trajectory (10000BC-2025)

JAGUAR resolves four structural demographic epochs across Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean Islands and Bermuda over the past twelve millennia (Figure 4 and Table 6). During the Palaeoindian and Archaic transition (10000BC-3000BC), hunter-gatherer and incipient horticultural populations across the 2,92M km² domain expanded from 480,1k in 10000BC (0,16 inhabitants/km²) and 649,0k in 8000BC to 1,39M in 6000BC, dipping during mid-Holocene arid phases to 900,2k in 5000BC and 1,10M in 4000BC before recovering to 1,72M by 3000BC. Early settlement clustered around highland lacustrine basins in central Mexico, Tehuacán, Oaxaca, coastal Veracruz and Chiapas estuaries, the Pacific Nicaraguan and Panamanian land bridge and early Lithic-Archaic shell-midden camps reaching Cuba and Hispaniola after 5000BC [@Cooke2005; @Fitzpatrick2015; @Siegel2015; @Nagele2020].

Sedentary maize agriculture, ceramic village networks and Formative state formation (3000BC-1AD) lifted gridded population from 1,87M in 2000BC to 2,93M by 1000BC (1,00 inhabitant/km²). Along the humid Gulf littoral, Olmec monumental centres at San Lorenzo and La Venta established the earliest Mesoamerican regional hierarchies, while Monte Albán consolidated the Valley of Oaxaca, Cuicuilco and Cholula expanded across central highland basins, and Pre-Classic Maya centres such as El Mirador and Nakbe rose across the karst Petén [@Diehl2004; @Pool2007; @Blanton1999; @PlunketUrunuela2012; @SharerTraxler2006]. Simultaneously, Ceramic Age Saladoid seafarers migrated northward from the Orinoco delta through Trinidad and the Lesser Antilles into Puerto Rico and Hispaniola, initiating dense horticultural village life across the islands [@Rouse1992; @Curet2005; @Boomert2016; @KeeganHofman2017].

```{r fig4-traj, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/jaguar_longrun_trajectory.png",
  "Long-run Holocene demographic trajectory of JAGUAR from 10000BC to 2025 on a semi-logarithmic scale (Panel A) and post-1500 linear trajectory from the colonial trough to modern expansion (Panel B).",
  "fig:holocene-traj"
)
```

During the Classic and Post-Classic millennia (1AD-1500AD), the gridded series records steady urban intensification punctuated by regional reorganisations. Domain population moved from 2,03M in 1AD and 2,03M in 500AD to 2,27M in 600AD, 2,43M in 800AD, 2,95M in 1000AD, 3,24M in 1200AD, 4,39M in 1400AD and a pre-contact crest of 4,99M in 1500AD (1,71 inhabitants/km²). Beneath that smooth macro-regional aggregate, constituent chapters capture sharp regional cycles: Teotihuacan grew to over 100k inhabitants in the Basin of Mexico before its sixth-century contraction [@Millon1973; @Cowgill2015; @Carballo2016]; Classic Maya population peaked across the central and southern lowlands around 700AD-800AD (Chapter 2 reaching 1,33M across 471,0k km², corroborated by airborne LiDAR terrace and causeway surveys across northern Guatemala and Belize) before Terminal Classic drought and political fragmentation shifted Maya demographic weight toward northern Yucatán and Mayapán [@Turner1990; @Webster2002; @Kennett2012; @ChaseChase2012; @Canuto2018; @MassonPeraza2014]. In central Mexico, Toltec Tula bridged the Epi-Classic transition before Late Post-Classic demographic expansion under the Aztec Triple Alliance and the Purépecha state lifted Chapter 3 to 3,20M by 1500AD, anchored on Tenochtitlan's chinampa-fed metropolitan basin [@Healan2012; @Calnek1972; @Offner1983; @Hassig1985; @Rojas2012; @Smith2012Aztecs]. Across Lower Central America and the Antilles, Chibchan chiefdoms (Chapter 4, peaking at 521,5k) and Ostionoid-Taíno cacicazgos (Chapter 5, 238,3k in the conservative gridded baseline) sustained dispersed coastal and interior agricultural hierarchies [@Helms1979; @Lange1992; @QuilterHoopes2003; @Sheets2002; @Joyce1991; @Whitehead1995].

```{r tab-macro-series, results='asis'}
sel_yrs <- c("-10000", "-6000", "-3000", "-1000", "0", "600", "1000", "1400", "1500", "1600", "1700", "1800", "1850", "1900", "1950", "1990", "2025")
```

## Conquest Collapse, Colonial Restructuring and Plantation Divergence (1492-1898)

The sixteenth century represents the deepest demographic contraction in the twelve-millennium series. In the gridded benchmark, domain population fell from 4,99M in 1500AD to 2,50M in 1600AD, a century-scale halving that conceals steeper short-run collapses documented in Chapters 6 and 9 between initial contact and the late sixteenth-century nadir [@BorahCook1963; @CookBorah1971; @Denevan1992; @Koch2019]. Across Mesoamerica and Central America (Chapter 6, dropping from 4,08M in 1518 to 2,99M by 1650 after deeper interim troughs in 1580-1620), successive waves of smallpox (1520), measles (1531) and *cocoliztli* epidemics (1545 and 1576) struck simultaneously with colonial *congregación* resettlement, tribute extraction and severe sixteenth-century drought [@Gibson1964; @Whitmore1992; @AcunaSoto2002; @Vagene2018; @Farriss1984; @Newson1987]. Across the Greater Antilles (Chapter 9), indigenous depopulation was virtually total within decades of Spanish settlement at La Isabela and Santo Domingo, leaving early colonial island totals reliant on modest Iberian and enslaved African arrivals until the mid-seventeenth century [@Sauer1966; @DeaganCruxent2002; @LiviBacci2003; @AndersonCordova2017; @AguirreBeltran1946].

Colonial demographic recovery reshaped the spatial geography of the entire macro-region between 1650 and 1821. In the Viceroyalty of New Spain (Chapter 7), gridded totals climbed from 1,78M in 1600 to 4,57M by 1820 as mestizo and recovered indigenous populations expanded across the Bajío, Guadalajara, Puebla, Michoacán and northern silver-mining provinces of Guanajuato, Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí [@Brading1971; @RabellRomero1990; @MinoGrijalva2001; @Humboldt1811]. In the Captaincy General of Guatemala (Chapter 8), population rose from 519,0k in 1600 to 1,25M in 1820 (peaking at 1,34M prior to late-colonial volcanic and epidemic shocks), centred on the Guatemalan highlands, Santiago de Guatemala, San Salvador and Costa Rica's Central Valley while Panama's transit economy fluctuated with transatlantic galleon traffic [@Lutz1994; @MacLeod1973; @JaenSuarez1978; @Wortman1982; @PerezBrignoli2010]. Meanwhile, the Colonial Caribbean Plantation Era (Chapter 10) transformed island demography from 475,4k in 1700 to 1,24M in 1890 through forced African migration (over four million captives disembarked across the Caribbean), creating extraordinarily dense sugar societies in French Saint-Domingue prior to the Haitian Revolution, British Jamaica and Barbados, and nineteenth-century Spanish Cuba and Puerto Rico [@EltisRichardson2010; @EngermanHigman1997; @Geggus1997; @Higman1984; @Roberts1957; @MoyaPons1995; @Nicholls1979].

## Modern Census Expansion and Urban Hierarchy Evolution (1821-2025)

Between 1850 and 2025, JAGUAR population expanded nearly twenty-eight-fold in the gridded series, from 7,23M in 1850 and 8,81M in 1890 to 17,67M in 1900 (when full national republican censuses replace colonial fiscal back-projections across Mexico, Cuba, Puerto Rico and Central America), 19,59M in 1910, 22,32M in 1920 (registering excess mortality and fertility deficits from the Mexican Revolution and the 1918 influenza pandemic), 27,18M in 1930, 33,16M in 1940 and 40,56M in 1950 [@McCaa2003; @Alba1982; @INEGICensos1996]. Post-1950 public health expansion, antibiotics, sanitation and rural-to-urban migration drove rapid demographic growth across all four modern macro-modules (Table 7): domain population surged to 60,27M in 1960, 77,89M in 1970, 105,92M in 1980, 137,20M in 1990, 164,88M in 2000 and 189,89M in 2010, before fertility decline and out-migration from Puerto Rico, Cuba and smaller islands slowed growth toward a peak of 208,18M in 2019 and a stabilised census level of 201,93M in 2025 [@CONAPO2023; @INEGuatemala2019; @INEHonduras2015; @INIDENicaragua2006; @INECCostaRica2023; @DIGESTYC2024; @SIBBelize2024; @ONEDomRep2023; @IHSIHaiti2015; @STATINJamaica2012; @USCensusPR2024].

Across the Lesser Antilles, Bahamas, Trinidad and Bermuda (Chapter 14), twentieth-century census series capture striking insular divergence: hydrocarbon industrialisation lifted Trinidad and Tobago above 1,3M, tourism and financial services expanded the Bahamas, Cayman Islands, Aruba and Bermuda, whereas volcanic eruptions on Montserrat after 1995 and sustained emigration held Dominica, Saint Vincent and Saint Kitts near modest twentieth-century ceilings [@CSOTrinidad2012; @NSIBahamas2023; @ESOCayman2022; @CBSAruba2022; @BSOBermuda2018; @BSSBarbados2023; @SDMontserrat2019; @CSODominica2012; @CSOGrenada2023; @CSOStLucia2023; @SOStVincent2014; @DSStKittsNevis2024; @SDAntigua2014; @ASDAnguilla2012; @CSOBVI2014; @DEPSTurksCaicos2014; @CBSCuracao2024; @CBSNethAntilles2002; @CBSNetherlands2025; @STATSintMaarten2018].

Sub-national spatial reallocation within the four contemporary modules was equally pronounced after 1950. Inside Mexico (Chapter 11, rising from 4,82M in 1830 to 118,78M in 2025 across 12.140 settlements), industrial manufacturing along the northern border corridor (Monterrey, Tijuana, Ciudad Juárez and Mexicali) and coastal tourism in Quintana Roo shifted growth away from purely central highland dominance even as the Valley of Mexico conurbation expanded beyond 20M inhabitants across unified Ciudad de México and its surrounding municipalities in Estado de México and Hidalgo [@Unikel1976; @Garza2003; @INEGICPV2021; @CONAPO2023]. Across the Central American Republics (Chapter 12, expanding from 1,17M in 1830 to 45,27M in 2025), dense highland and Pacific piedmont belts in Guatemala, El Salvador and Costa Rica's Central Valley contrasted sharply with sparsely populated Caribbean rainforests in Petén, Mosquitia, eastern Nicaragua and Darién, while Panama's demographic mass remained tightly anchored along the trans-isthmian corridor between Panama City and Colón [@INEGuatemala2019; @DIGESTYC2024; @INEHonduras2015; @INIDENicaragua2006; @INECCostaRica2023; @INECPanama2023; @SIBBelize2024]. In the Greater Antilles (Chapter 13, 805,6k in 1840 to 36,95M in 2025), post-1980 trajectories diverged sharply: rapid demographic ageing and emigration slowed Cuba and reduced Puerto Rico from its 2004 peak, whereas Haiti and the Dominican Republic sustained strong natural increase across Hispaniola [@ONEICuba2014; @DiazBriquets1983; @USCensusPR2024; @VazquezCalzada1988; @IHSIHaiti2015; @ONEDomRep2023; @STATINJamaica2012].


Rank-size analysis of the 15.401 settlement trajectories reveals a long-run structural steepening of the urban hierarchy across JAGUAR (Figure 5). Pre-Columbian lowland and archipelagic settlement systems without a single imperial capital exhibited shallow rank-size slopes: $\alpha = 0,45$ ($R^2 = 0,97$) in Lower Central America, $\alpha = 0,46$ ($R^2 = 0,97$) in the Pre-Columbian Caribbean and $\alpha = 0,69$ ($R^2 = 0,99$) across the polycentric Classic Maya lowlands. By contrast, highland imperial basins already displayed steep primacy, with $\alpha = 1,09$ ($R^2 = 0,88$) in Chapter 1 (dominated by Teotihuacan) and $\alpha = 0,86$ ($R^2 = 0,75$) in Late Post-Classic Mexico (dominated by Tenochtitlan). During the colonial period, administrative decentralisation across *audiencias*, silver-mining towns and competing island sugar ports kept rank-size exponents moderate ($\alpha = 0,62$ to $0,90$, including $0,67$ across 826 settlements in New Spain). Modern industrialisation, railway networks and post-1950 metropolitan primacy pushed every modern chapter close to or above classic Zipf scaling: $\alpha = 0,95$ in Mexico after Independence (12.140 settlements anchored by unified Ciudad de México, Guadalajara, Monterrey, Puebla and Tijuana), $\alpha = 0,92$ in Central America, $\alpha = 1,05$ in the Greater Antilles (Havana, Santo Domingo, Port-au-Prince, San Juan and Kingston) and $\alpha = 0,95$ across the Lesser Antilles, Bahamas, Trinidad and Bermuda [@Unikel1976; @Garza2003; @Chandler1987; @Modelski2003].

```{r fig5-urban, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/jaguar_urban_hierarchy_evolution.png",
  "Rank-size Zipf exponent evolution across all 14 JAGUAR chapters by era (Panel A) and cross-era upward shift in the top-100 Mexican settlement hierarchy from Pre-Columbian Mesoamerica to 2025 (Panel B).",
  "fig:urban-hierarchy"
)
```

## Comparative Benchmarking against Global Historical Compendia

Benchmarking JAGUAR against global historical demographic reconstructions illustrates both macro-level alignment and decisive sub-regional refinement (Table 8). For the pre-contact millennia, JAGUAR's gridded trajectory (2,93M in 1000BC, 2,03M in 1AD, 2,95M in 1000AD and 4,99M in 1500AD) sits squarely within the conservative-to-moderate range of global baselines such as McEvedy and Jones (1978), Maddison (2001) and HYDE 3.2, while individual chapter syntheses document higher regional peak estimates in the Basin of Mexico, Oaxaca and the Classic Maya lowlands where archaeological settlement surveys and LiDAR coverage support denser local reconstructions [@McEvedyJones1978; @Maddison2001; @KleinGoldewijk2017; @Denevan1992; @Canuto2018].

The decisive gain of JAGUAR lies in spatial distribution between 1000BC and 1950. Rather than projecting twentieth-century Mexican states, post-1903 Canal Zone divisions or modern Caribbean metropolitan densities backward onto pre-industrial landscapes, JAGUAR anchors prehistoric surfaces on 11.970 audited archaeological sites and dual HYDE 3.5 plus KK10 land-use priors, then transitions across 29 strictly non-anachronistic administrative regimes tied to 3.785 primary colonial and republican enumerations. Consequently, the resulting 5-arcminute rasters preserve the Classic Maya lowland peak and Terminal Classic shift to Yucatán, the sixteenth-century divergence between depopulated tropical lowlands and highland Mesoamerican cores, the eighteenth-century Bajío mining boom and Antillean plantation surge, and modern metropolitan clustering around unified Ciudad de México, Monterrey, Guadalajara, Guatemala City, San José, Havana and Santo Domingo.

# Limitations

Four structural limitations merit transparent documentation for downstream spatial modellers and historians. First, prehistoric and contact-eve population totals across Mesoamerica and the Caribbean remain one of the most contested quantitative debates in historical demography [@BorahCook1963; @Henige1978; @Denevan1992; @Brooks1993; @LiviBacci2003]. While non-stationary Matérn kriging over 11.970 regional archaeological sites constrains relative spatial gradients far more tightly than biophysical priors alone, absolute domain totals prior to 1500AD carry substantial structural uncertainty ($\pm 30\%$ to $\pm 50\%$ across highland Mesoamerica and wider relative intervals in Hispaniola and the Maya lowlands depending on household occupancy multipliers and site contemporaneity assumptions). Readers examining high-count versus low-count contact estimates should consult Chapters 1 through 6 and Chapter 9 directly, where both conservative gridded totals and upper-bound archaeological reconstructions are tabulated side by side.

Second, archaeological survey coverage remains uneven across environments. Open highland basins (the Basin of Mexico and Valley of Oaxaca) and extensively mapped Maya zones (FAMSI MayaGIS and UCSB Maya Forest GIS) yield dense site registries, whereas humid Caribbean rainforests in Mosquitia, eastern Panama, Darién and portions of Cuba and Haiti suffer from lower ground-survey visibility and heavier reliance on radiocarbon anchors (accounting for the Caribbean's 79,06% regional monograph share versus 99,95% in Mexico and 99,56% in Central America). Dual HYDE 3.5 and KK10 covariates mitigate under-surveyed zones during kriging, yet small interior islands and dense tropical canopies retain wider local prediction variance than surveyed Mexican basins.

Third, transition discontinuities appear in the continuous gridded series where historical statistical regimes shift abruptly, most visibly between 1890 (8,81M) and 1900 (17,67M), and in minor census-to-projection adjustments between 2019 (208,18M) and 2020 (200,79M). The 1890-1900 step reflects the simultaneous entry of full national sub-administrative census tables across Mexico (1895/1900), Cuba (1899), Puerto Rico (1899) and Central America replacing coarser colonial and nineteenth-century fiscal interpolations in the underlying global baseline; researchers analysing continuous nineteenth-century national growth rates should therefore rely on the individual country census tables compiled in Chapters 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14 rather than differencing raw gridded sums across the 1890-1900 boundary.

Fourth, historical sub-administrative boundary resolution expands progressively over time. While modern snapshots deploy 302 to 307 active sub-administrative units with up to 263 direct census enumerations, early colonial snapshots between 1500 and 1750 necessarily rely on coarser *audiencia*, provincial and island-level polygons (27 to 59 active units), delegating intra-provincial rural allocation to the kriged archaeological and environmental suitability surfaces.

# Conclusion

JAGUAR establishes an integrated, bottom-up historical population reconstruction across 2,92M km² spanning Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean Islands and Bermuda from 10000BC to 2025. By uniting 14 chronological and regional chapters, 238 unique open-access scholarly PDFs, 11.970 primary archaeological sites (plus 1.248 CENTAUR northern frontier buffer sites) calibrated via non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging across 1.673 dual HYDE 3.5 and KK10 catchments, 29 strictly non-anachronistic historical GIS administrative regimes covering all 118 Common Era HYDE steps with pycnophylactic mass conservation ($5,76 \times 10^{-8}$ worst unit relative error) and 15.401 evidence-only settlement trajectories preserving unified Ciudad de México and 699 extra-municipal suburbs, JAGUAR resolves persistent spatial anachronisms in global historical gridding. All 128 output population rasters are harmonised along the 322-pixel northern CENTAUR seam for direct integration into pan-American and global Holocene demographic syntheses.

# Appendix

All 14 constituent regional chapters are organised into three thematic directories under JAGUAR: Pre-Columbian societies (Chapters 1-5: Mesoamerica to 1200AD, Classic and Post-Classic Maya Lands, Aztec Empire and Late Post-Classic Mexico, Lower Central America and Pre-Columbian Caribbean Islands), Conquest and Colonial regimes (Chapters 6-10: Conquest and Collapse in Mexico and Central America, Viceroyalty of New Spain, Captaincy General of Guatemala, Spanish Conquest of the Indigenous Caribbean and Colonial Caribbean Plantation Era) and Modern and Census jurisdictions (Chapters 11-14: Mexico after Independence, Central American Republics, Greater Antilles in the Modern Era and Lesser Antilles, Bahamas, Trinidad and Bermuda). Each chapter directory archives its paired literature review and settlement gazetteer manuscripts, equal-area raster and vector sub-regional masks, machine-readable settlement trajectories, source saturation ledgers, visual inspection records and open-access PDF bibliography.
